questions.prompt: Approximately how many seconds are in a day?
questions.explanation: A day is 24 x 60 x 60 = 86,400 seconds, roughly 10^5 — a handy shortcut for turning per-day numbers into per-second (QPS).

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson of the classic latency numbers?

options.text: All storage is about equally fast
Memory is far faster than SSD, which is far faster than disk, and a cross-continent round trip dwarfs local work
Network calls are always faster than memory access
Disk seeks are measured in nanoseconds

questions.explanation: The ratios matter: memory (~100 ns) << SSD (~tens of microseconds) << disk seek (~10 ms), and a cross-continent round trip (~150 ms) dominates. That is why we cache and use CDNs.

questions.prompt: A service handles 40 writes/second. Assuming a 100:1 read-to-write ratio, what is the approximate read QPS?
questions.explanation: read QPS = write QPS x read:write ratio = 40 x 100 = ~4,000 reads/second.

questions.prompt: Because traffic is spiky, you should always size a system for its ______ load, not its average. (one word)
questions.explanation: Sizing for the average under-provisions; apply a peak factor (often 2-3x) and design for the peak.

questions.prompt: Which factors belong in a storage estimate? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Storage = items x size per item x retention x replication factor. Forgetting replication is a common way to undercount by a factor of 2-3.

questions.prompt: What makes a back-of-the-envelope estimate trustworthy and defensible?

options.text: Reporting the number to several decimal places
Stating the assumptions behind it so others can check them

questions.explanation: The value is order-of-magnitude, not precise. Stated assumptions are what let others verify and challenge the estimate.
